key_terms.meaning: A substance with one fixed chemical composition throughout, e.g. water, nitrogen; it may exist in more than one phase but each phase has the same composition
Liquid at a pressure above the saturation pressure for its temperature; also called subcooled liquid
Liquid exactly at the boiling point for its pressure, with no vapour present, quality x = 0
Vapour exactly at the boiling point for its pressure, just about to condense, quality x = 1
Vapour at a temperature higher than the saturation temperature for its pressure
A three-dimensional surface that shows all equilibrium states of a pure substance; two-phase regions appear as surfaces, single-phase regions as volumes
The single pressure and temperature at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium; for water 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa
The end point of the liquid-vapour saturation curve; for water 647.1 K (374 °C) and 220.6 bar, where latent heat falls to zero
Heat absorbed by 1 kg of saturated liquid to become saturated vapour at constant pressure and temperature, h_fg = h_g − h_f
x = mass of dry vapour ÷ total mass of wet mixture, so 0 ≤ x ≤ 1; x = 0 saturated liquid, x = 1 saturated vapour
Tabulated values of h_f, h_g, h_fg, v_f, v_g, s_f and s_g against pressure and temperature for water and steam
An h-s diagram of steam on which isobars, isotherms, constant-x lines and constant-v lines are drawn, used for graphical reading of properties and processes
A device that throttles wet steam to a low pressure so it becomes superheated; h before equals h after, which gives x
A gas whose molecules occupy no volume and exert no forces except during collision; obeys pv = RT with R = R̄/M
(p + a/v²)(v − b) = RT, where a/v² is the attraction correction and b the molecular volume correction, with v the molar volume
Z = pv/RT; Z = 1 for an ideal gas, and departure from 1 measures the error of the ideal gas approximation
For an ideal gas mixture the total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures: p = Σp_i, with p_i = y_i p
y_i = n_i/n = N_i/N, the number of moles of component i divided by the total moles in the mixture
ω = m_v/m_a = 0.622 p_v/(p − p_v), kilograms of water vapour carried by 1 kg of dry air
A plot of moist air properties — dry-bulb temperature, humidity ratio, relative humidity, enthalpy — from which the state point gives all the others

takeaways: All equilibrium states of a pure substance lie on its p-v-T surface, and the two-phase region is only a surface or a line, not a volume.
The triple point is a single point for a given substance; the critical point closes the liquid-vapour curve and removes the difference between liquid and vapour.
Inside the wet region pressure and temperature are not independent — fixing one fixes the other, so a second property such as x is needed to fix the state.
Enthalpy of wet steam follows h = h_f + x·h_fg, and the same mixing rule applies to v, s and u with v_f, v_g and s_f, s_g.
Steam tables and the Mollier chart are read, not solved; they replace the missing equation of state for water in exam problems.
A throttling calorimeter relies on the fact that h is constant across a throttle, and it works only when the steam is dry enough to leave superheated.
Real gases depart from pv = RT near saturation and at high pressure; Z = pv/RT, read from the generalised chart with reduced properties, quantifies that departure.
In an ideal gas mixture each component behaves as if alone in the vessel, so the mixture calculations reduce to weighted sums using mole fractions.
Moist air is treated as an ideal gas mixture of dry air and water vapour, which is why the psychrometric chart carries two independent temperatures.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are almost always numerical plus a diagram: a labelled p-v-T or T-h sketch with the tables and the Mollier chart actually read to produce h, v, s and Z, so the syllabi expect the method and the numbers together, not one without the other.

bank.q: Draw the p-v-T surface of water and explain what every region and every line on it represents. Show how the p-v and T-v diagrams are obtained from it as projections.
outline: Solid, liquid and vapour single-phase volumes separated by two-phase surfaces
Triple point is a line in p-T and a point on the p-v projection; three phases coexist there
Fusion curve for water slopes backwards because water expands on freezing
Vapourisation surface ends at the critical point; beyond it no distinction between liquid and vapour
Sublimation surface lies below the triple point
Constant-temperature and constant-pressure lines on the surface become the isotherms and isobars of the p-v and T-v diagrams

bank.q: Define triple point and critical point. Give their values for water and explain why the liquid-vapour saturation curve ends at the critical point.
outline: Triple point: unique (p, T) where solid, liquid and vapour coexist; water 273.16 K, 611.7 Pa
Critical point: highest (p, T) at which liquid and vapour phases differ; water 647.1 K, 220.6 bar
Latent heat of vaporisation falls to zero at the critical point
Surface tension vanishes and the densities of the two phases become equal
Above the critical isotherm a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone

bank.q: Explain the formation of steam at constant pressure from 0 °C water to superheated steam. Show the process on a T-h and an h-s diagram, and define sensible heat, latent heat, dryness fraction and degree of superheat.
outline: Sensible heating of liquid from 0 °C to saturation temperature, h_f
Evaporation at constant temperature absorbing h_fg
Superheating of vapour, extra enthalpy h − h_g
Dryness fraction x marks the position along the evaporation line
Degree of superheat = T − T_sat at the given pressure
Diagram: liquid line, evaporation line, superheat region with isobars for two pressures

bank.q: State Dalton's law of partial pressures and Amagat's law of additive volumes. For an ideal gas mixture show that the mole fraction equals the volume fraction and that p_i = y_i·p.
outline: Dalton: p = Σp_i with each gas at the mixture volume and temperature
Amagat: V = ΣV_i with each gas at the mixture pressure and temperature
Ideal gas for each component: p_i V = n_i R̄ T
Divide component equation by mixture equation to get p_i = y_i p
Volume fraction V_i/V equals n_i/n = y_i
Validity only for ideal gas mixtures at moderate pressure

bank.q: Steam at 10 bar has a dryness fraction of 0.90. Using steam tables (h_f = 762.8 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2015.3 kJ/kg, v_f = 0.001127 m³/kg, v_g = 0.1944 m³/kg) find h, v and u of 1 kg.
outline: Note that v_f is small but not zero and u is not h

bank.q: Steam at 8 bar passes through a throttling calorimeter and leaves at 1 bar, 120 °C. Using h_f = 721.1 kJ/kg and h_fg = 2046.5 kJ/kg at 8 bar, and h = 2716.4 kJ/kg for steam at 1 bar, 120 °C, find the dryness fraction of the main steam.
outline: Throttling is adiabatic with no work, so h₁ = h₂
h₂ = 2716.4 kJ/kg from superheated values at 1 bar, 120 °C
State the assumption of steady flow, negligible kinetic and potential energy, and no heat loss

bank.q: One kilogram of carbon dioxide is held in a 0.05 m³ vessel at 300 K. Calculate the pressure using (i) the ideal gas equation and (ii) the van der Waals equation (a = 364.3 kPa·m⁶/kmol², b = 0.0427 m³/kmol), and comment on the difference.
outline: n = 1/44 kmol, R = 0.1889 kJ/kg·K
van der Waals: p = nR̄T/(V − nb) − a n²/V²
nb = 0.00097 m³, so first term ≈ 1156 kPa
Attraction term ≈ 75 kPa, giving p ≈ 1081 kPa
Real pressure is below ideal because attraction dominates at this moderate density

bank.q: A gas mixture has the volumetric analysis CO₂ 12%, O₂ 8%, N₂ 80%. For the mixture find the molar mass, the gas constant, the mass fractions and the partial pressure of each gas at 1 bar, 300 K.
outline: Mass fraction of CO₂ = y M_i/M = 0.12×44/30.24 = 0.1746, similarly for others
p_i = y_i p: CO₂ 0.12 bar, O₂ 0.08 bar, N₂ 0.80 bar
Volume fraction = mole fraction for an ideal gas mixture

bank.q: Moist air at 1 atm has a dry-bulb temperature of 30 °C and a wet-bulb temperature of 20 °C. Using the psychrometric chart, find relative humidity, humidity ratio, dew-point temperature, specific enthalpy and specific volume.
outline: Locate the state at the intersection of DBT 30 °C and WBT 20 °C
Read relative humidity from the curved lines, about 53%
Read humidity ratio on the right-hand scale, about 0.014 kg/kg dry air
Follow the horizontal line left to saturation to read dew point, about 19.5 °C
Read enthalpy from the oblique scale through the state point
Read specific volume from the constant-v lines

bank.q: Explain physically why a real gas deviates from pv = RT. Derive the van der Waals constants a and b in terms of critical properties and show how the equation predicts the critical point.
outline: Two assumptions break down: molecules have finite volume, and they attract each other
b corrects the volume, a/v² corrects the pressure
At the critical point the isotherm has an inflection: (∂p/∂v)_T = 0 and (∂²p/∂v²)_T = 0
Solving the three critical-point equations gives v_c = 3b, T_c = 8a/(27Rb), p_c = a/(27b²)
Therefore a = 27R²T_c²/(64p_c) and b = RT_c/(8p_c)
Predicted Z_c = 3/8 = 0.375 for all substances, against 0.23–0.31 measured — a known weakness

bank.q: A throttling calorimeter reads reliably only when the main steam is fairly dry. Explain why, and describe how a combined separating and throttling calorimeter extends the range.
outline: After throttling the steam must be superheated, otherwise its state is still two-phase and its enthalpy cannot be found from temperature alone
Very wet steam cannot be superheated enough by a small pressure drop
Separating calorimeter removes most of the water mechanically and gives an approximate x from the separated masses
The remaining almost-dry steam is then throttled and its x found by the enthalpy balance
Overall x combines the two stages: x = x_sep × x_throttle style relation on the vapour masses

bank.q: With the help of the psychrometric chart, explain sensible heating, sensible cooling, cooling and dehumidification, and evaporative (adiabatic) cooling of moist air. Give one air-conditioning use of each.
outline: Sensible heating: horizontal line, humidity ratio constant, DBT and enthalpy rise — winter room heater
Sensible cooling: horizontal line to the left until saturation — coil above dew point
Cooling and dehumidification: line bends down along the saturation curve, both DBT and humidity ratio fall — summer coil below dew point
Evaporative cooling: constant wet-bulb line, DBT falls and humidity ratio rises — desert cooler
Apparatus dew point and bypass factor may be mentioned as extra detail

bank.q: Compare steam tables, the Mollier chart and a throttling calorimeter as ways of obtaining the enthalpy of wet steam in a plant trial. State the accuracy, speed and range of each and recommend one for a routine boiler test.
outline: Tables: most accurate inside the printed range, interpolation needed, slow by hand
Mollier chart: fast for combined processes and expansions, reading error of the order of a few kJ/kg
Calorimeter: measures the actual steam in the pipe, so it captures the true x including carry-over, but needs dry-enough steam and instruments
Recommendation: calorimeter for x, tables or chart for the rest of the properties, chart for sketching the process
Sources of error: heat loss in the throttle, kinetic energy, gauge errors, interpolation

bank.q: Saturated steam at 150 °C has p_sat = 4.758 bar and v_g = 0.3925 m³/kg. Compute the specific volume from pv = RT, find Z, and judge whether the ideal gas law can be used for steam near saturation.
outline: R for steam = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K, T = 423.15 K, p = 475.8 kPa
Ideal v = RT/p = 0.4104 m³/kg
Error in v is about 4.6%, in the same direction as condensation tendency
Conclusion: acceptable for rough work at low pressure, not acceptable when h or mass flow must be accurate; use tables or a real-gas equation near the dome

glossary.def: Another name for dryness fraction; the vapour mass fraction in a saturated liquid-vapour mixture.
Heat that changes the temperature of a single phase without changing the phase, equal to m·c·ΔT for a constant specific heat.
The difference between the actual temperature of superheated steam and the saturation temperature at the same pressure.
The amount by which a liquid is cooler than its saturation temperature at the given pressure.
The boiling or condensing temperature that belongs to a given pressure for a pure substance.
The pressure at which a pure substance boils at a given temperature.
A mixture of saturated liquid droplets and saturated vapour in equilibrium, with 0 < x < 1.
Steam with x = 1, containing no liquid droplets, at the saturation temperature for its pressure.
Steam above its saturation temperature for the given pressure; it behaves roughly as a gas.
h_fg, the heat needed to convert 1 kg of saturated liquid into saturated vapour at constant pressure.
A gas whose behaviour departs from pv = RT because its molecules have volume and interact.
p_r = p/p_c, the pressure divided by the critical pressure of the substance.
T_r = T/T_c, the absolute temperature divided by the critical temperature.
All substances at the same reduced pressure and temperature have nearly the same compressibility factor Z.
The volume of an ideal gas mixture equals the sum of the volumes each component would occupy at the mixture pressure and temperature.
The pressure a single component of a gas mixture would exert if it alone filled the same volume at the same temperature.
Air with the water vapour removed; it is the reference mass for humidity ratio calculations.
φ = p_v/p_sat at the dry-bulb temperature, the ratio of actual vapour pressure to the saturation value.
The temperature at which moist air becomes saturated when cooled at constant pressure and humidity ratio.
The ordinary temperature of moist air measured by a thermometer with a dry bulb.
The temperature reached by a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in wet cloth and exposed to moving air.
A steady-flow expansion through a restriction with no work and negligible heat transfer, so enthalpy stays constant.
